# Running a Study

::: {.callout-note}

-   Design an ethically sound study that fits a workplace.
-   Use Goal-Question-Metric to turn a vague worry into a measurable question.
-   Scope a study to what you can actually run.
-   Match a question to the method, and push for better evidence.

:::

Meridian's team has learned enough to be dangerous. They know the vendor's
studies have holes, they know how to watch five people, and they know how to
design a real experiment. The last thing standing between them and an answer is
everything that isn't the research: ethics, politics, and the discipline of
turning "is the tool worth it?" into something with a number on the end.

A 2014 survey of practitioners found they most wanted questions like "how do I
improve team productivity?" answered with *their own data from their own systems*
— not controlled experiments or interviews with strangers [@Begel2014]. That's
the frame for this chapter: you already have most of what you need; the skill is
using it well.

## Ethics First

Research on people needs ethical care even when it's "internal." "It's just
internal data" is not a free pass — the fact that you already have access doesn't
make using it harmless. {{<g informed_consent "Informed consent" >}} means people
know what's collected and how it's used and can withdraw without consequence —
and "it's in the employment contract" is *not* consent, because the alternative
is leaving the job.

When monitoring developers, even with consent, store data locally or give
participants control over what's shared. Monitoring that erodes the
psychological safety that predicts team performance defeats the study before it
starts. And get legal and HR involved *before* you collect individual-level data;
retroactive approval is harder than proactive review.

## Start with Your UX Team

If your organization has a UX (user research) team, give this job to them. UX
researchers already do rigorous qualitative work — interviews, think-aloud
sessions, thematic analysis — and rigorous quantitative work — usability metrics
and the statistics to interpret them. They are already trained to ask "does this
actually help people do their work?", so an AI assessment program is not a new
project for them; it's their existing job pointed at a new tool.

If you don't have a UX team, the earlier chapters are the toolkit you would
otherwise hand them: the [cheap-and-fast lesson](../cheaply/index.qmd) for
formative think-aloud and RITE studies, and the [study-design
lesson](../design/index.qmd) for the statistics to interpret the results.
If you *do* have a UX team but want to check or follow along with their work, the
checklist in the [reading-studies lesson](../critical/index.qmd) is what you use
to sanity-check their conclusions. Either way, get someone *outside* your
organization to challenge whether your metric actually measures what you care
about.

## Scoping the Question with GQM

"Does AI make our developers more productive?" can't be answered until you know
what "productive" means, which developers, on which tasks, over what period. The
{{<g gqm "Goal-Question-Metric" >}} approach forces the issue [@Basili1994]:

-   **Goal** — what object, what property, from whose viewpoint, in what context?
-   **Questions** — whose answers would tell you whether the goal was met.
-   **Metrics** — the specific, operationalized number for each question.

For Meridian: *Goal* — understand the AI assistant's effect on delivery speed,
from the engineering manager's view, in the current sprint process. *Question
1* — does time-to-merge change after adoption? *Metric 1* — median hours from PR
open to merge, per sprint. *Question 2* — does defect rate change? *Metric 2* —
bugs filed within 14 days of a merge.

A scoped question looks like: *"Did time-to-first-review decrease for PRs
submitted after we deployed the tool, compared to the three months before?"*
One team, one metric, one comparison, one period. If that scoped question doesn't
answer what stakeholders actually need to know, you've learned something
important *before* running the study.

## Practical Designs You Can Actually Run

Most practitioners can't run a randomized trial — no random assignment, no
control group, limited time. The realistic alternatives:

-   {{<g retrospective_analysis "Retrospective analysis" >}} — study what already
    happened with data you already have (commit logs, tickets, review comments).
-   **Interrupted time series** — treat a policy or tool change as a natural
    experiment, looking for a trend change at the change point.
-   {{<g internal_survey "Internal survey" >}} — a structured survey of your own
    team, with clear scope and honest limitations.
-   {{<g ab_testing "A/B testing" >}} — if you ship software, random assignment
    of users to conditions is often already in your infrastructure.

Be honest about which design you actually have, not which you wish you had. And
invest no more than a quarter of your budget in the first run — the first study
rarely answers the question you thought you were asking, and a negative result
often tells you what the *real* question is.

## Sharing Results Without Overselling

Every study has limitations; state them before stakeholders ask. Distinguish
"we found no effect" from "our study wasn't designed to detect an effect."
Put confidence intervals, effect sizes, and sample sizes in the report, not just
the appendix. And ask, before you send anything, "what happens if this appears
on Reddit?"

When you can't publish, write a memo with methods, results, limitations, and
conclusions — and share it with the team that was studied, not just the
leadership that commissioned it.

## Matching Methods to Questions

As a quick reference:

-   "Is there a difference?" → controlled experiment or quasi-experiment.
-   "How large is the difference?" → effect sizes and confidence intervals.
-   "Why does this happen?" → interviews and observation.
-   "What do practitioners think?" → surveys.
-   "What patterns exist in our codebase?" → mining repositories.
-   "What causes what?" → natural experiments, DiD, ITS — or randomization.

The hardest step is usually the first: translating a vague worry ("is AI bad for
us?") into a specific, answerable question.

## What the Evidence Actually Says (and What's Oversold)

Stepping back, the honest summary of AI-productivity research is short: AI tools
can speed up specific, well-defined tasks for individual developers; effects on
end-to-end delivery are far less studied and less consistent; and nearly all
studies are short-term, on narrow or artificial tasks, with volunteers or
students. The "55% faster" headline is a task-level result being sold as a
workday-level fact.

So when an executive cites a statistic, ask three questions: *who funded it,
what task was studied, and was there a control group?* And when it's your turn to
buy a tool, ask for evidence from a context like yours — not students on toy
tasks — with effect sizes and confidence intervals, on outcomes you actually care
about.

## Signs of Maturity

A team that has stopped asking "does the tool work?" and started asking harder
questions is on the right track. Watch for these three:

1.  "How am I going to be measured in my annual performance review?"
2.  "What do we keep when token costs go up 20×?"
3.  "How much should I spend on insurance, and for what?"

The first keeps the tool from becoming a surveillance device; the second keeps
you from building your workflow on a cost you don't control; the third
acknowledges liability for generated code. A team asking these is treating AI as
a business decision, not a fad.

None of these traps are unique to AI. The same problems — proxy metrics, no
control group, selection bias, overclaiming — appear in studies of agile, TDD,
and every other practice, and they're as old as empirical software engineering
itself. The fix is to apply what the human sciences already know — which, as
above, is usually already sitting in your UX team.

## Misconceptions

Internal data has no ethical constraints because the company already owns it.
:   Collecting data for operations doesn't authorize using it for research. The
    intended use matters, and research use needs separate consent and harm review.

A/B testing is a reliable all-purpose tool for internal studies.
:   It works when random assignment is natural and outcomes are measured
    automatically. Most questions about developer productivity don't fit.

Negative results aren't worth reporting.
:   A well-run null result prevents acting on a false assumption. Suppressing it
    recreates the file-drawer problem inside your own organization.

The evidence on AI and developer productivity is settled.
:   The field is young, dominated by short-term narrow studies, heavily
    industry-funded, and almost entirely lacking independent replication.

## Check Understanding

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">Why is "it's in the employment contract" insufficient as a basis for consent?</summary>

Consent must be specific, informed, and genuinely voluntary. An employment
contract grants broad data-collection rights as a condition of employment, so
participants can't meaningfully withdraw without leaving their job — a power
imbalance that undermines voluntariness.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">A manager asks you to study "which developers are least productive" using commit data. Name two ethical concerns and one fix for each.</summary>

Commit data has low construct validity and can be gamed — use outcome metrics
(defect rate, feature delivery time) instead of activity metrics. And ranking
"least productive" individuals risks surveillance and discipline — commit in
advance that results are for process improvement, not performance management.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">A colleague says "hundreds of studies show AI improves productivity — the evidence is overwhelming." What's the key concern?</summary>

Publication bias: positive results get published, null results don't. A large
count of positive studies may just mean the negative ones are in file drawers. A
meta-analysis that corrects for publication bias would give a more reliable
picture than a head count.

</details>

## Exercises

### Scope It Down (15 minutes, pairs)

Take one broad question — "does using an AI assistant improve code quality?",
"does test-driven development reduce bugs?", "does remote work hurt
collaboration?" — and write a scoped version answerable in three months with a
typical team's data. Specify the metric, the comparison, and the time period.

### Write the Limitations (20 minutes, solo)

You ran an internal A/B test: 30 developers used an AI code-review tool for eight
weeks, 30 didn't, and time-to-merge fell 22% in the treatment group. Write the
"Limitations" section — sample size and power, external validity, alternative
explanations, and ethics.

### The Question Behind the Question (15 minutes, pairs)

A manager says, "We're spending $X per developer per year on this AI tool. Are we
getting our money's worth?" Restate it as three specific, answerable research
questions. For each, name the method and one data source. Then say which question
matters most and why.
